items.rawSummary: Negotiations remain deadlocked as Iran demands full sanctions relief, compensation for U.S. military actions, and refuses to tie a war-ending deal to nuclear commitments, while the U.S. and Israel reportedly prepare for possible renewed attacks.
items.analysis: State television continued airing live weapons demonstrations even as President Pezeshkian urged mosques to promote austerity and called for “dignified” dialogue with Washington. A revised Iranian proposal relayed through Pakistan demands a permanent ceasefire, full sanctions relief, full access to frozen assets, and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, while deferring detailed nuclear talks to later stages, a senior Iranian source told Reuters; Washington has offered only a phased release of 25% of frozen funds and limited relief, underscoring the gap. The New York Times reported that the U.S. and Israel are preparing for a possible resumption of attacks as early as this week, echoing an informed European source’s assessment that many officials see imminent U.S. military action. Iran’s foreign ministry expressed deep suspicion toward talks, reaffirmed a right to impose passage fees in the Strait of Hormuz, and warned against U.S. interference in the World Cup. The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency reported that Iran demanded compensation for U.S. military actions, described U.S. demands as unrealistic, and rejected any linkage between ending the conflict and nuclear commitments. A senior Iranian source later told Reuters that Tehran will not agree under any circumstances to linking an end to the war with nuclear commitments, further widening the deadlock.

items.rawSummary: U.S.-Iran diplomacy remains at an impasse after Washington rejected Tehran's revised proposal as insufficient, while both sides prepare for a potential resumption of military action.
items.analysis: President Trump told Fortune that Iran's latest offer contained 'nothing to do with what we agreed on,' and the White House formally rejected it, with Axios reporting that a senior official warned negotiations may now continue 'through bombs.' The New York Times detailed intensive U.S.-Israeli military preparations for possible attacks as early as this week, while an American source told Al Jazeera that Iran has only days remaining. President Trump is expected to convene his top national security team in the Situation Room on Tuesday to discuss military options. Meanwhile, Iranian state media Tasnim claimed Washington offered a temporary oil sanctions waiver during talks, though U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent called on the G7 to enforce sanctions tightly. Domestically, U.S. CPI inflation is on track to exceed 5% this year, potentially reaching 5.2% by the November midterms, adding economic pressure to an already fraught diplomatic landscape.

items.rawSummary: Following the Trump-Xi summit, China confirmed plans to purchase U.S. planes and lower some tariffs, while its Foreign Ministry reiterated its claim over Taiwan and Russia scheduled a presidential visit to Beijing.
items.analysis: The visit yielded agricultural and energy purchases and Trump's claim of a 200-plane Boeing commitment, later confirmed by China's Commerce Ministry alongside tariff reductions and assurances on U.S. agricultural concerns. Trump said tariffs and Taiwan were not discussed, and he raised the Jimmy Lai case to a negative response. According to the New York Post, the U.S. delegation took extreme counterintelligence measures, discarding all Chinese gifts and using burner phones. On the Strait of Hormuz, the leaders expressed a desire to reopen the waterway, but Xi gave no specific undertaking, while PRC-linked vessels continue to transit under Iranian-asserted routing, potentially normalizing Tehran's claim to control the strait. The Kremlin announced Putin will visit Beijing on May 19-20, extending the trip and underscoring Beijing's effort to balance deeper economic ties with Washington against its alignment with Moscow. US Treasury Secretary Bessent described the talks as successful. In a subsequent statement, China's Foreign Ministry declared Taiwan an inalienable part of its territory and said independence is irreconcilable with cross-strait peace, reinforcing Beijing's long-standing position after Trump said he made no commitment on the island's status.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz area (Bandar Abbas vicinity), Iran: An unverified claim circulated that Iran opened the Strait of Hormuz, sought a truce with the U.S., and signaled openness to a long-term nuclear freeze but not removal of enriched uranium.
items.description: An unverified claim circulated that Iran opened the Strait of Hormuz, sought a truce with the U.S., and signaled openness to a long-term nuclear freeze but not removal of enriched uranium.
items.rawSummary: Commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains at a near standstill, with Iran extending its institutional control through a new strait management body and a Bitcoin-backed insurance service, while U.S. forces have shifted from enforcement operations to planning the next phase of efforts to reopen the waterway.
items.analysis: Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has collapsed to fewer than five vessels per day, down from a pre-war norm of about 130, as Iran deepens its administrative and financial grip. Tehran has formally created a management body for the strait and launched 'Hormuz Safe,' a Bitcoin-backed insurance product initially offered to Iranian shipping companies and cargo owners, which the government says could generate more than $10 billion in revenue. U.S. Central Command reports that a total of 85 vessels have been intercepted under the blockade—81 redirected and four disabled—and House Speaker Johnson stated that Operation Epic Wrath has concluded while planning for a successor project to reopen the strait is underway. An unverified claim circulated that Iran had opened the strait and sought a truce with the United States, signaling openness to a long-term nuclear freeze but not removal of enriched uranium; however, this contrasts with Tehran’s simultaneous moves to impose transit fees and insurance requirements, and no official confirmation has emerged. Senator Graham urged a tougher posture, and while alternative overland routes through China, Pakistan, and Iraq are being expanded, they cannot replace the volume of seaborne trade, and the disruption is raising concerns about drug shortages in Europe.

items.title: Nearby Iranian positions (implied operational area), Iran: The Institute for National Security Studies published an assessment by Maj. Gen. (res.) Tamir Hayman concluding that despite tactical gains, Israel failed to stop Iran's regime survival and nuclear advancement; Iran repaired facilities, accelerated work at underground sites, and decentralized command to ensure continuity.
items.description: The Institute for National Security Studies published an assessment by Maj. Gen. (res.) Tamir Hayman concluding that despite tactical gains, Israel failed to stop Iran's regime survival and nuclear advancement; Iran repaired facilities, accelerated work at underground sites, and decentralized command to ensure continuity.
items.rawSummary: Diplomatic efforts to resolve the Iran standoff remain deadlocked as U.S. and Israeli officials prepare possible strikes, while a detailed new assessment argues that Iran’s regime and nuclear program have proven resilient despite the 2025 war, and the nationwide internet blackout stretches into its 80th day.
items.analysis: U.S. and Israeli officials continue to finalize targets for possible strikes on Iran, with President Trump warning on May 17 that time is running out, while exiled opposition figure Reza Pahlavi urged him to seize the moment to 'finish the job.' Negotiations remain stuck over war reparations, sanctions relief, and the transfer of enriched uranium. Amid these tensions, an assessment published by the Institute for National Security Studies, authored by Maj. Gen. (res.) Tamir Hayman, contends that Israel achieved tactical gains in the 2025 conflict but failed to prevent the survival of the Iranian regime or the progress of its nuclear program — Iran rapidly repaired facilities like Fordow, accelerated work at buried sites, and decentralized its command so field officers could launch missiles and close the Strait of Hormuz without waiting for orders. The assessment adds that Iran’s leadership succession to Mojtaba Khamenei occurred without a vacuum, and that the closure of Hormuz shifted Washington’s priorities toward protecting energy markets. These findings complicate the picture of Iran’s military posture, contrasting with earlier U.S. claims of collapsing command and control, even as China exerts economic pressure and concerns rise that Iran could threaten submarine internet cables to disrupt global banking and trade. An 80-day internet blackout persists inside Iran, with most citizens cut off from outside communication while state-controlled access reaches a select few.

items.rawSummary: Negotiations remain deadlocked as Iran demands full sanctions relief, compensation for U.S. military actions, and refuses to tie a war-ending deal to nuclear commitments, while the U.S. and Israel reportedly prepare for possible renewed attacks.
items.analysis: State television continued airing live weapons demonstrations even as President Pezeshkian urged mosques to promote austerity and called for “dignified” dialogue with Washington. A revised Iranian proposal relayed through Pakistan demands a permanent ceasefire, full sanctions relief, full access to frozen assets, and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, while deferring detailed nuclear talks to later stages, a senior Iranian source told Reuters; Washington has offered only a phased release of 25% of frozen funds and limited relief, underscoring the gap. The New York Times reported that the U.S. and Israel are preparing for a possible resumption of attacks as early as this week, echoing an informed European source’s assessment that many officials see imminent U.S. military action. Iran’s foreign ministry expressed deep suspicion toward talks, reaffirmed a right to impose passage fees in the Strait of Hormuz, and warned against U.S. interference in the World Cup. The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency reported that Iran demanded compensation for U.S. military actions, described U.S. demands as unrealistic, and rejected any linkage between ending the conflict and nuclear commitments. A senior Iranian source later told Reuters that Tehran will not agree under any circumstances to linking an end to the war with nuclear commitments, further widening the deadlock.
